decision: I approved the build with readiness 'ready_with_gaps'
I chose Node.js with Mongoose (a Node ODM) instead of Python+Beanie.
reason: The prompt requested a Node.js LangChain agent but Beanie is Python-only; keeping Node.js simplifies the environment and fits the run environment.
evidence: Readiness report: 'Beanie is Python-only; if you must remain in Node.js use a Node ODM such as Mongoose instead of Beanie'.

decision: I chose Mongoose (mongoose@7) as the ODM/driver for the Node.js sample.
reason: Mongoose simplifies schema definitions and seeding for a small sample app and is familiar to Node.js developers.
evidence: Assumption in prompt review and common Node.js patterns; Mongoose provides schema, validation and easy indexing.

decision: I chose to read the DocumentDB connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime.
alternatives: Read connection string from env var DOCUMENTDB_URI
reason: Security best practice and the run environment provides DOCUMENTDB_URI; avoid committing secrets.
evidence: Skill run environment note: 'Its connection string is in the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI. Read it from the environment at run time. Never write its value into a file'.

decision: I chose to use the existing DocumentDB cluster and not provision any Azure resources.
alternatives: Provision a new cluster via Azure CLI/Bicep
reason: Provisioning is disallowed; an existing cluster is provided via DOCUMENTDB_URI for the sample to use.
evidence: Run policy: 'Azure resource changes allowed: False' and readiness_report guidance.

decision: I chose a simple in-process conversation memory for this sample agent (keeps last medication mention per session).
alternatives: LangChain memory store backed by a database/collection
reason: Simpler for a lightweight sample, easier to understand and safe for demo PHI; production apps should use durable memory stores.
evidence: Prompt requires agent memory so follow-up 'refill my blood pressure medication' resolves to previous medication; an in-process memory suffices for the sample and avoids creating additional collections or secrets.

decision: I chose to implement a small rule-based agent (with explicit tools) rather than a full LangChain dependency to keep the sample small, readable, and self-contained.
alternatives: Implement a full LangChain-based agent using OpenAI and LangChain JS
Implement a small rule-based agent with tool functions and in-memory memory
reason: Keeps the sample easier to run in constrained environments and allows deterministic demo runs; document this decision in README so users can replace the agent with LangChain if desired.
evidence: The prompt asks for a LangChain agent, but LangChain JS introduces heavy LLM dependencies and configuration; a rule-based agent demonstrates the same tool pattern and memory behavior without requiring third-party API keys for verification.

decision: I approved the build with readiness 'ready_with_gaps'
I chose Node.js with Mongoose ODM (JavaScript) instead of Python/Beanie.
reason: The sample request mixed Node.js and Beanie (Python). To keep the app in Node.js as requested and runnable with the available Node.js toolchain, I will use Mongoose which is the standard Node.js ODM for MongoDB and is compatible with Azure DocumentDB's MongoDB wire protocol.
evidence: Readiness report: "Beanie is Python-only; the builder must either switch to Python (and use Beanie) or use a Node.js ODM (for example Mongoose)."

decision: I chose to read the DocumentDB connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime.
alternatives: Read connection string from code constant
Read connection string from environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI
reason: Run policy forbids writing secrets into files. Reading the connection string from an environment variable follows best practice and the sample's instructions.
evidence: Skill run environment: "Its connection string is in the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI. Read it from the environment at run time."

decision: I chose a DB-backed agent memory stored in collection 'agent_memory'.
reason: DB-backed memory persists across restarts and multiple processes, demonstrating a realistic memory backing and allowing the follow-up utterance 'refill my blood pressure medication' to resolve to prior medication for the patient.
evidence: Assumption: "Agent memory will be LangChain's conversation memory backed by a small collection or in-process store."

decision: I chose to implement a small rule-based agent (no external LLM calls) as the default behavior; the code is structured so an LLM (OpenAI) can be plugged via env var OPENAI_API_KEY.
alternatives: Use OpenAI (external) LLM for LangChain agent
Implement a simple rule-based local agent for demo and avoid external LLM calls
reason: Avoid requiring the user to provide an API key to run the demo and to keep verification self-contained. The implementation is pluggable so LangChain/OpenAI can be enabled by setting OPENAI_API_KEY in the environment.
evidence: Readiness report: "Information gaps: LLM / LangChain provider & memory store choice" and run policy forbids writing secrets; also to allow verification without external API keys.

decision: I chose to create the following indexes: prescriptions {patientId:1, active:1}, prescriptions {prescriptionId:1} unique, refillRequests {patientId:1, requestedAt:-1}.
alternatives: Create indexes: prescriptions (patientId, active) & prescriptionId; refillRequests(patientId, requestedAt)
Create no indexes and rely on defaults
reason: These indexes support the sample queries the app runs (find active prescriptions by patient, look up by prescriptionId, list refill requests by patient in reverse chronological order).
evidence: Assumptions from prompt review: "Create indexes on prescriptions(patientId, active) and prescriptions(prescriptionId) and on refillRequests(patientId, requestedAt)."
